content: Welchol (colesevelam hydrochloride) is a bile acid sequestrant used to treat primary hyperlipidemia and type 2 diabetes mellitus. It is not absorbed systemically and works by binding bile acids in the intestine, reducing their reabsorption. This depletion of bile acids leads to increased cholesterol conversion to bile acids in the liver, upregulation of LDL receptors, and a subsequent reduction in serum LDL cholesterol levels. However, triglyceride levels may increase or remain unchanged. Welchol is FDA-approved for reducing elevated LDL cholesterol in adults with primary hyperlipidemia as an adjunct to diet and exercise. It can be used alone or in combination with statins. It is also approved to improve glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus, though it is not indicated for type 1 diabetes or diabetic ketoacidosis. The drug has not been extensively studied in combination with dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors or thiazolidinediones, nor in pediatric patients with type 2 diabetes. Welchol is contraindicated in patients with a history of bowel obstruction, serum triglyceride levels >500 mg/dL, or a history of hypertriglyceridemia-induced pancreatitis. It may increase triglyceride levels, and lipid parameters should be monitored before and during treatment. If triglycerides exceed 500 mg/dL or if pancreatitis develops, the drug should be discontinued. Patients with triglyceride levels >300 mg/dL should be treated with caution. Welchol may interfere with the absorption of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, and K) and certain drugs. Patients on oral vitamin supplementation should take their vitamins at least 4 hours before Welchol. Similarly, drugs with known interactions or narrow therapeutic indices should be administered at least 4 hours prior to Welchol. The safety and efficacy of Welchol have been evaluated in clinical trials involving patients with primary hyperlipidemia and type 2 diabetes. Common adverse reactions include constipation, dyspepsia, nausea, and abdominal pain. In lipid-lowering trials, 68% of patients on Welchol reported adverse reactions compared to 64% on placebo. In type 2 diabetes trials, 60% of patients on Welchol reported adverse reactions compared to 56% on placebo. Gastrointestinal side effects were the most common reason for discontinuation. Welchol has not been shown to reduce cardiovascular morbidity or mortality. Its effects on macrovascular outcomes remain unproven. In animal studies, colesevelam hydrochloride did not demonstrate carcinogenicity, mutagenicity, or impairment of fertility. Reproductive toxicity studies in rats and rabbits revealed no evidence of fetal harm. Welchol is classified as Pregnancy Category B. While animal studies have shown no fetal harm, there are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women. The drug should be used during pregnancy only if clearly needed. It is not expected to be excreted in human milk due to its lack of systemic absorption. For pediatric patients aged 10 to 17 years with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, Welchol has been shown to reduce LDL cholesterol levels. However, it has not been studied in children younger than 10 years or in premenarchal girls. The adverse reaction profile in pediatric patients was similar to that in adults. Welchol is available as tablets or oral suspension. The oral suspension should be mixed with water, fruit juice, or diet soft drinks before ingestion and taken with meals. Due to the large tablet size, patients with swallowing difficulties are advised to use the oral suspension. Lipid levels should be monitored within 4 to 6 weeks of initiating therapy. In summary, Welchol is an effective treatment for lowering LDL cholesterol and improving glycemic control in specific patient populations. However, its use requires careful monitoring of lipid parameters, potential drug interactions, and patient-specific contraindications.
